page.title: Work.
page.intro: Where I've worked, and what I've built along the way.

filmin-smart-tv.title: Filmin on your TV
filmin-smart-tv.headline: One app, every television.
filmin-smart-tv.summary: The Filmin app on televisions from 2016 to today, all from one React codebase. These days I'm the one leading the smart TV side.
filmin-smart-tv.intro: Filmin is Spain's home for independent film and series. I work on its television app: one React codebase running on Samsung, LG, Hisense, Android TV, Fire TV, Vega OS, Vodafone and PS4, on sets from 2016 to the ones in shops today. Having been on it the longest, I've grown into leading the smart TV team.

smart_details.name: My part
smart_details.description: Leading the smart TV app, day to day

smart_details.name: Alongside
smart_details.description: Backend, product, design, encoding and editorial

smart_details.name: Rhythm
smart_details.description: Four to six weeks per idea

points.title: The problem
points.name: A TV is kept for a decade
points.description:
People keep a television far longer than a phone, so the app has to feel just as good on a 2016 Samsung as on a set bought last week. That 2016 Samsung runs an engine as old as Chrome 23, with a fraction of a laptop's memory.
Under the hood it's still web development — the app is React running in a webview — just with a much wider range of browsers to respect.

points.title: The approach
points.name: Compatible first, then scalable
points.description: Every change has to work on the oldest set we support and still leave room for the next platform to arrive. Most of the craft is in keeping both of those true at the same time.
quotes: A deliberate polyfill strategy instead of shipping everything everywhere
CSS workarounds for old engines, kept isolated and documented
Performance measured on the slowest device, not the average one
Platform quirks consolidated, so one feature ships to every TV at once

points.title: The team
points.name: Product first, then code
points.description:
I like to think of myself as a software engineer with a product mindset. Knowing the product well — and what each television will actually take — lets me be useful early, in the room with product and design, before an idea becomes something we'd have to undo.
We work closely with the backend, product, design, encoding and editorial teams, and I try to make the smart TV side an easy team to work with.

points.title: The role
points.name: Growing into the lead
points.description: Over time I've grown into leading the smart TV side: keeping an eye on priorities, making sure nothing on the TV side falls through the cracks, and being the person product and design can come to with any question about televisions.

angular-to-react.title: From Angular to React
angular-to-react.headline: Changing the engine mid-flight.
angular-to-react.summary: Moving the TV app from Angular to React while it kept shipping every few weeks. More about patience and good sequencing than speed.
angular-to-react.intro: When I joined, the TV app was built in Angular and tied to an older project, with years of special cases for televisions that disagreed with each other. Today it's fully React — and we got there without ever stopping releases.

smart_details.name: Built with
smart_details.description: React, with Angular beside it until the end

smart_tags.name: Coexistence
smart_tags.description: Both frameworks in one build, for a while

points.title: The problem
points.name: A rewrite nobody could pause for
points.description: The comfortable way to change frameworks is to stop everything and do only that. A streaming service can't: new features, device certifications and fixes all keep their own calendar. So the migration had to happen inside our normal release rhythm, or not at all.

points.title: The approach
points.name: Sequence over speed
points.description: First we untangled the app from the older project so it could stand on its own. Then we moved it piece by piece, with both frameworks living in the same build until the last Angular view was gone. Every piece that crossed over left some of its special cases behind.
quotes: Decoupled from the legacy project before touching the UI
Migrated gradually, both frameworks sharing one build
Platform-specific branches cleaned up as they crossed over
The oldest TVs kept working throughout — Chrome 23 included

points.title: The result
points.name: Quietly done
points.description: Angular is gone. One React codebase ships to every television at once, and the energy we used to spend keeping two worlds alive now goes into the product.

vega-os-launch.title: Filmin on Amazon Vega OS
vega-os-launch.headline: From the SDK to the store.
vega-os-launch.summary: Amazon's brand-new TV platform, with nobody to ask and nothing to search. I read the SDK, worked out what it could do and took Filmin all the way to the store.
vega-os-launch.intro: Vega OS is Amazon's move away from Android on its TVs — so new that when something didn't work, there was nothing to search. I evaluated the SDK, mapped what the platform would and wouldn't support, adapted our app and took it through to store submission.

smart_details.name: Rhythm
smart_details.description: Reading the SDK before writing code

smart_tags.name: SDK evaluation
smart_tags.description: What the platform can really do

smart_tags.name: Capability map
smart_tags.description: What could stay, what had to change

smart_tags.name: Adaptation
smart_tags.description: The React app, fitted to Vega

points.title: The problem
points.name: Nothing to search for
points.description: Mature platforms come with years of other people's questions already answered. Vega came with an SDK and not much else, and nobody at the company had shipped on it yet.

points.title: The approach
points.name: Read first, build second
points.description: Before changing anything, I read the SDK and made a map of what the platform supported and what our app took for granted. That map shaped the work: what could stay, what needed adapting, and what to ask Amazon about directly.
quotes: SDK evaluation before a line of app code
A map of what Vega would and wouldn't support
The existing React app adapted, not rewritten
A direct line to Amazon for what the docs didn't cover

points.title: The launch
points.name: All the way to the store
points.description: Adapted, submitted and released through Amazon's store. Seeing Filmin live on a platform that didn't exist for us a few months earlier was a very good day.

banking-widgets.title: Chat with your bank manager
banking-widgets.headline: A person, not a queue.
banking-widgets.summary: The in-app chat CaixaBank customers use to talk with their bank manager, built in a team where developers worked side by side with people from the financial side.
banking-widgets.intro: At CaixaBank Tech most of my time went into one feature: the chat that lets customers talk with their bank manager in the app. We were a team of seven or eight people with very different roles — developers, some of them remote in Valencia, working every day with colleagues from the financial side. Along the way I also built a small Stencil widget.

smart_details.name: My part
smart_details.description: The app side of the manager chat

smart_details.name: Alongside
smart_details.description: Financial roles, and developers in Valencia

smart_tags.name: Manager chat
smart_tags.description: Customers talking with their bank manager

smart_tags.name: Mixed team
smart_tags.description: Developers and financial roles, side by side

points.title: The product
points.name: Talking to a person
points.description: For a lot of customers, the most valuable thing a bank can offer is still a person who knows them. The chat brought that into the app: a direct line to your own manager, without phone calls or trips to the branch. My part was the app side — the conversation itself and everything around it.

points.title: The team
points.name: Learning the other side
points.description: Many of the people I worked with every day weren't engineers. Working next to colleagues in financial roles taught me to ask why before how, and to explain technical trade-offs in plain words. The developers were spread across different cities, so clear written communication mattered just as much.

points.title: The rest
points.name: Small pieces, handled with care
points.description: Next to the chat I built a Stencil widget — a small, framework-agnostic component other teams could drop into their products. In banking every release reaches a lot of people very quickly, so shipping carefully became a habit rather than a rule.

keolis-sites.title: Websites for Keolis
keolis-sites.headline: Small teams, many sites.
keolis-sites.summary: Consultancy work for Keolis, the international public transport operator: keolis.com, its tourism and innovation portals and more, built in small teams between Spain and France.
keolis-sites.intro: At Extia my client was Keolis, an international public transport operator. I worked with developers in Spain and in France, always in English, grouped into small teams of two or three that moved between projects — keolis.com, the tourism portal, the innovation portal and others.

smart_tags.name: DatoCMS
smart_tags.description: Content the client's editors could own

points.title: The context
points.name: Working in English, across borders
points.description: It was my first international team. Everything happened in English — standups, reviews, the small talk — which felt like a big step at first and quickly became normal. It's still one of the things I'm most glad I did early on.

points.title: The work
points.name: Many sites, small teams
points.description: We were split into teams of two or three and moved between Keolis projects as they came up. Small teams meant everyone touched everything: structure, components, content and the details that make a site feel finished.
quotes: keolis.com, the tourism portal, the innovation portal and more
Gatsby with React and TypeScript, often from an empty repository
Content modelled in DatoCMS and queried over GraphQL
Code reviews and Jest tests as part of the routine

points.title: The takeaway
points.name: Shipping as a team
points.description: Two or three people sharing a codebase leaves little room for ego. Reviewing each other's work, agreeing on conventions and handing projects over cleanly taught me more about teamwork than any single project did.

flykube-eatkube.title: Flykube & Eatkube
flykube-eatkube.headline: Where it all started.
flykube-eatkube.summary: My first job: an internship that turned into a contract, building the Flykube and Eatkube websites and the Eatkube app — back when the tech team was the CTO and me.
flykube-eatkube.intro: This is where it started for me — first as an intern, then hired. When I joined, the whole tech team was the CTO and me, working hand in hand with design and product. The team grew over time, and so did I.

smart_details.name: My part
smart_details.description: Websites in React, the app in React Native

smart_details.name: Built with
smart_details.description: React, React Native and a little Django

smart_tags.name: Django
smart_tags.description: Small tasks, a first taste of backend

points.title: The context
points.name: A team of two
points.description: For a while the whole tech team was the CTO and me. That meant working directly with design and product, learning fast and getting used to owning things early. As more people joined, I got to watch a small company find its shape.

points.title: The work
points.name: Two websites and an app
points.description: I built the Flykube website and the Eatkube website in React, and the Eatkube app in React Native. Eatkube was a food delivery app built around surprise. I don't think it exists anymore, but I still like the idea.

points.title: The takeaway
points.name: A first look at the backend
points.description: I wasn't a backend developer, but I picked up some small Django tasks along the way. Nothing big — just enough to see how a real production backend works, and it has shaped how I think about the frontend ever since.

griselhub.title: GriselHub
griselhub.headline: The studio the apps ship under.
griselhub.summary: The independent iOS studio behind Crescia, Yantar and Fulcrum. One site carrying the shared identity, the store listings and the legal pages every app has to link to.
griselhub.intro: Three apps on the App Store need somewhere to point. Apple requires a privacy policy and a support URL per app, and shipping them as three unrelated names leaves nothing behind. GriselHub is the studio those apps ship under, and the site that serves all of it.

smart_details.name: Languages
smart_details.description: EN, ES, CA, DE, FR, IT, PT

smart_tags.name: Legal pages
smart_tags.description: Privacy, terms and support per app

points.title: The problem
points.name: Three apps, no shared home
points.description:
Crescia, Yantar and Fulcrum were shipped separately, and each one needed a privacy policy and a support page before Apple would take it. Three sets of legal pages on three throwaway URLs is duplicated work that ages badly. 
It also meant three unrelated names with nothing tying them together, so nothing compounded between releases.

points.title: The approach
points.name: One studio, one site
points.description:
GriselHub is the name all three ship under, and the site does the shared jobs: the studio front, the store links, and the privacy, terms and support pages each app points at from its App Store listing. 
It runs in seven languages, matching where the apps are actually sold rather than defaulting to English.

points.title: The result
points.name: The next app inherits it
points.description: Shipping the fourth app is now a listing and a section rather than a new site. The privacy and support obligations are already met, and each release adds to one name instead of starting another.

fulcrum.title: Fulcrum
fulcrum.headline: Point a camera at dinner.
fulcrum.summary: A training log and calorie tracker for iOS and Apple Watch. Photograph a meal and a vision model reads back the foods, the grams and the calories.
fulcrum.intro: Fulcrum is a training log for people who build their own routines, with calorie tracking attached. No preset programs and no coaching. The one place a model earns its keep is the part nobody wants to do by hand: typing in what you just ate.

smart_details.name: My part
smart_details.description: Design, iOS, watchOS and the server

smart_tags.name: Meal scan
smart_tags.description: Photo in, foods and calories out

smart_tags.name: Routine builder
smart_tags.description: Your own exercises, your own days

smart_tags.name: Watch sessions
smart_tags.description: Log every set from the wrist

smart_tags.name: On-device data
smart_tags.description: No account, no sync, no ads

points.title: The problem
points.name: Calorie tracking is data entry
points.description:
Every calorie app is a search box. You eat something, then you spend two minutes describing it to a database that does not have it. Most people stop within a week, and the training log they came for dies with it. 
 The training side had the opposite problem: plenty of apps, all of them convinced they should pick your programme for you.

points.title: The approach
points.name: A model for the boring part only
points.description:
Fulcrum builds the routine side the plain way: your own exercises, your own weekdays, rest timers, personal records the moment you beat them, and the whole session runnable from the watch. 
 The model is pointed at the one job it is genuinely better at. You photograph the plate, the image goes to Claude, and it comes back as structured items with grams and calories that you confirm or correct. No chat, no coach, no feed.

points.title: The server
points.name: The key never ships in the app
points.description:
An API key inside a binary is a key you have given away, so the app never holds one. Scans go through a small Cloudflare Worker that keeps the key as a server secret, caps the image size, and rate limits per IP so a leaked app token cannot become somebody else’s bill. 
 It is about a hundred lines of TypeScript and it sits in the free tier.

crescia.title: Crescia
crescia.headline: Every record stays with you.
crescia.summary: A personal finance app that keeps every record on the device. Design, build and release start to finish — product decisions included.
crescia.intro: A personal finance app with one rule: records live on the device and in the owner's own iCloud — no server of mine ever holds them. Designed, built, shipped and marketed by one person.

smart_details.name: My part
smart_details.description: All of it — design, build, release, marketing

smart_tags.name: Statement import
smart_tags.description: Bank statements parsed with the Claude API

smart_tags.name: iOS widget
smart_tags.description: A place on the home screen

smart_tags.name: ASO
smart_tags.description: Listing tuned in Spanish and English

points.title: The problem
points.name: Finance apps ask for too much
points.description: The default trade in personal finance is convenience for custody: connect your bank, create an account, and a copy of your financial life lives on somebody's server. Crescia refuses the trade — records stay on the device and in the owner's own iCloud, and nowhere else.

points.title: The build
points.name: One person, every hat
points.description: SwiftUI and SwiftData underneath, iCloud as the only sync. The features that usually justify a server had to be solved without one.
quotes: Bank statement import, parsed with the Claude API
Subscriptions through StoreKit, tested in sandbox before anyone paid
An iOS widget for the home screen
SwiftData persistence, syncing through the owner's iCloud alone

points.title: The store
points.name: The part nobody warns you about
points.description: App Store Connect has its own curriculum: a monthly subscription rejected in review, a product ID reserved permanently by a mistake you can't undo, and the release cycles in between. The distance between writing an app and shipping one lives here.

points.title: The reach
points.name: Marketing is part of the product
points.description: A shipped app nobody finds is a side project. ASO across the Spanish and English listings, Instagram campaigns measured with funnel analysis, and a featuring nomination submitted to Apple.

yantar.title: Yantar
yantar.headline: The first one out the door.
yantar.summary: A fasting tracker with the same rule: nothing leaves the phone. Built and published end to end.
yantar.intro: A fasting tracker for iOS with the rule Crescia later kept: everything stays on the phone. The first app I took the whole way — idea, design, build, review, release.

smart_tags.name: Design
smart_tags.description: The interface was half the project

smart_tags.name: App Store
smart_tags.description: First pass through review and release

points.title: The itch
points.name: A timer that minds its own business
points.description: Fasting trackers tend to arrive with accounts, streaks and a server watching. Yantar is the simple version: track the fast, keep the data on the phone, ask for nothing.

points.title: The build
points.name: Design as half the work
points.description: A tracker this small lives or dies on its interface — there's no feature list to hide behind. SwiftUI, and more hours in the design than the data model.

points.title: The lesson
points.name: What shipping teaches
points.description: The first full pass through App Store review, release and everything around it. What it taught carried straight into Crescia — which is the point of shipping a first app at all.

andreafrancin.title: Andrea Francin
andreafrancin.headline: A portfolio that its owner can run.
andreafrancin.summary: A portfolio site for an illustrator, with a custom back office so she publishes her own work without touching code or waiting on me.
andreafrancin.intro: Andrea is an illustrator. The brief was a portfolio that looks like her work and that she can keep current on her own, in two languages, without a developer in the loop.

points.title: The problem
points.name: Most illustrator portfolios go stale
points.description:
The work changes constantly, the site does not. Either the artist pays someone every time a project lands, or the site slowly stops representing them. 
 Andrea needed the opposite: a site she could update the afternoon she finished something.

points.title: The approach
points.name: A back office built for one person
points.description:
A Django REST backend with authentication and a PostgreSQL store, and a React frontend that reads from it. Projects, images and copy are all editable from a private admin, with a markdown editor for longer text. 
 Every project carries both language versions, so translating is part of writing rather than a separate job.

points.title: The result
points.name: She has not needed me since
points.description: The site is live and she maintains it herself. The part I am pleased with is not the stack, it is that the handover actually held.
